How to Write Wedding Vows: A Simple Structure, Prompts and Examples

Learn how to write personal wedding vows with a clear structure, reflection prompts and examples. Make promises that sound authentic to your relationship.

Personal wedding vows do not need to sound poetic or perfect. They need to express what you value about your partner and the commitments you are ready to make. A useful structure is: what you love, one meaningful memory, what partnership means to you and a few promises you can genuinely keep.

Special Occasions8–10 min readUpdated 7 November 2026
Written by RA FahimWishly Guide Editorial

Quick answer

Set aside time to reflect, choose two or three specific details, and write promises that describe how you intend to show up in the marriage. Read the draft aloud, keep it within the ceremony’s agreed time and confirm any religious, cultural or officiant requirements before finalising it.

  • Describe your partner using details only you would naturally notice.
  • Write promises about actions and values, not only big feelings.
  • Agree on length, tone and ceremony requirements with your partner or officiant.

Understand what a vow is meant to do

A wedding vow is a promise made in the context of a marriage ceremony. It may be traditional, religious, civil or personally written, depending on the couple and the ceremony. Before drafting, ask your officiant or ceremony organiser whether any wording is required and whether there is a time limit.

Personal vows are different from a speech or a toast. They can include a memory or a little humour, but their centre should be the commitments you are making and the respect you intend to bring to the partnership.

Collect details before writing

Write privately for ten or fifteen minutes about the qualities you admire, a moment when you felt supported, something you learned together and what you hope to build. Do not edit while collecting ideas. Specific details will make the final wording feel more personal than broad statements about destiny or perfection.

Consider asking yourself: What do I appreciate that I do not say often? What did we learn during a difficult season? What does being a reliable partner mean in daily life? What kind of home, friendship or future do we hope to create?

  • A quality you admire and a moment that showed it.
  • A shared memory that captures your relationship.
  • A value you want to protect as life changes.
  • A promise that can be seen in everyday behaviour.

Use a simple four-part structure

Begin with a direct statement about the person you are marrying. Add a brief memory or observation that explains why the relationship matters to you. Then name the values you want your marriage to reflect, such as patience, honesty, humour, care or shared responsibility.

Finish with two to four promises. Make them specific enough to guide your actions: listening before reacting, sharing responsibilities, making time for one another, supporting individual goals or returning to difficult conversations with respect. Avoid promises that depend entirely on circumstances outside your control.

Write promises that are honest and sustainable

Grand language can be beautiful, but vows become meaningful through follow-through. Instead of promising that every day will be happy, promise to communicate honestly when a day is difficult. Instead of promising never to disagree, promise to handle disagreement without contempt and to seek understanding.

Choose commitments that match your values and capacity. You can promise effort, kindness, support and a willingness to learn. You cannot guarantee that no challenge will happen or that either person will never change.

Edit the draft for sound, length and privacy

Read your vows aloud. Replace phrases that feel borrowed, shorten sentences that are difficult to speak and check that any joke will be comfortable in front of the audience. Ask your partner whether they prefer similar lengths or a shared tone, while keeping the exact wording a surprise if that is part of the tradition.

Be careful with private stories. A wedding ceremony may include family, friends and children. Do not reveal a partner’s sensitive experience or share personal photos and messages without permission. A small, respectful reference can be meaningful without exposing something private.

A fill-in outline to get started

Use this outline as a drafting aid and then rewrite it in your own words: “I love the way you [specific quality]. I still remember [shared moment], because it showed me [what it means]. I want our marriage to make room for [values]. I promise to [action], to [action], and to keep learning how to [shared goal].”

The outline is not a finished vow. Replace every bracket with something accurate, remove any line that does not feel true and check ceremony requirements before you print or memorise the final version.

Frequently asked questions

How long should wedding vows be?

Follow the ceremony organiser’s guidance. Many couples choose a short passage that can be spoken comfortably in about one to two minutes, but the agreed format matters more than a fixed word count.

What should I include in personal wedding vows?

Include what you appreciate about your partner, a meaningful observation or memory, the values you want to share and practical promises you intend to keep.

Should wedding vows be funny or romantic?

They can include both if that tone feels right to you and your partner. Keep humour kind and avoid private jokes that could embarrass someone.

Can I use a wedding vow template?

A template can help organise ideas, but rewrite it with real details and promises that reflect your relationship. Check any ceremony rules before using it.
